newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court to hear religious freedom law case.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court to hear religious freedom law case.

text.p: The Supreme Court will hear arguments Wednesday in an important constitutional challenge to a 1993 federal law that created greater protection from government regulation for the exercise of religious rights.

The justices will consider whether Congress overstepped its legislative authority in adopting the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, a measure which President Clinton strongly supported and signed into law.

The law prevents federal, state and local governments from placing a substantial burden on the exercise of a sincere religious practice. The government must cite a "a compelling interest" to justify the regulation and must adopt the least restrictive means possible.

The law was aimed at encouraging governments to accommodate religious practices. The standard set by the law created a much higher hurdle for government regulation than what the Supreme Court decided in a controversial 1990 ruling.

The parties challenging the law said Congress had no authority to adopt a measure governing local claims about religion. They charged the law also dictates to the states to accommodate religion more than what the Constitution requires.
Besides important church-state issues, the case also raises profound questions about federalism and the separation of powers between the various branches of government.
The case arose after Boerne, Texas denied an application from a Catholic archbishop for a permit to expand a church because of its location within the city's historic district.
Citing a large increase in parishioners, the church said it would be unable to accomplish its mission and survive as a parish church unless it expanded.
The archbishop sued, claiming denial of the construction permit violated the 1993 law. The city replied that the law was unconstitutional.
A federal judge struck down the law, but a U.S. appeals court upheld it as constitutional, resulting in the city appealing to the Supreme Court.

The Clinton Justice Department strongly defended the law, saying it protects the First Amendment rights for the free exercise of minority religions and deters governmental violations of religious rights.

The law "ensures that minority, unpopular and emerging faiths enjoy the same freedom as religious adherents who possess the political means to obtain legislative exemptions from burdensome laws," Acting Solicitor General Walter Dellinger said.
A coalition of more than 60 religious and civil liberties groups also voiced support for the law.

"Accommodation under (the law) is available to all religious practitioners, without regard to their size or political clout. (It) treats all religions equally," they said in a court brief filed with the high court.

But a group of 16 state attorney generals complained the law has been abused by prisoners who have demanded special food, clothing and other privileges by claiming it was part of their religious beliefs.
After the arguments, the justices will take the case under advisement, with a decision by the end of June.
